hints: Let $p$ be the probability that Jill hits the target on one shot. $\text{H}_0$ says nothing has changed from last week's 65%. Jill claims she has improved, so decide which way $\text{H}_1$ points (one-tailed).

Under $\text{H}_0$ the number of hits in 20 shots is $X \sim \text{B}(20, p)$ with $p$ the $\text{H}_0$ value. A result as good as 18 hits or better is what counts, so you need $\text{P}(X \geqslant 18) = \text{P}(18) + \text{P}(19) + \text{P}(20)$.
Use the binomial formula ${}^{20}\text{C}_r \, p^r q^{20-r}$ for $r = 18, 19, 20$ (or the binomial pdf function on your calculator) and add the three, giving the total to 3 s.f.
Compare your probability with the significance level, 1%, written as a decimal. Is your probability smaller or larger?
Reject $\text{H}_0$ only if your probability is smaller than the significance level. Then write the conclusion in the context of Jill and her shooting, using cautious wording rather than certainty.
walkthrough:
**Set up the hypotheses (earns the B1)**

A hypothesis test starts with a default belief, $\text{H}_0$, and then asks whether the data give strong enough evidence against it. Let $p$ be the probability that one of Jill's shots hits the target.

Last week 65% of her shots hit, which as a decimal is $0.65$. The default belief is that she has not changed. Jill claims she has **improved**, which means $p$ is bigger. That makes the test one-tailed (we only care about an increase).

$$\text{H}_0: p = 0.65$$

$$\text{H}_1: p > 0.65$$

**Say which distribution applies if $\text{H}_0$ is true**

Each shot is independent, there are only two outcomes (hit or miss) and, if $\text{H}_0$ is true, the chance of a hit is the same $0.65$ every time. The number of hits in 20 shots is therefore binomial.

$$X \sim \text{B}(20, 0.65)$$

**Choose the probability to work out**

Jill hit 18 out of 20. To judge whether that is surprising we ask: if $\text{H}_0$ were true, how likely is a result **at least this good**? That means 18, 19 or 20 hits. (Using only $\text{P}(X = 18)$ would ignore the even more impressive results.)

$$\text{P}(X \geqslant 18) = \text{P}(X = 18) + \text{P}(X = 19) + \text{P}(X = 20)$$

**Write the three terms (this earns the M1)**

The binomial formula is $\text{P}(X = r) = {}^{20}\text{C}_r \times 0.65^r \times 0.35^{20-r}$, where $0.35 = 1 - 0.65$ is the chance of a miss.

$$\text{P}(X = 18) = {}^{20}\text{C}_{2} \times 0.35^2 \times 0.65^{18}$$

$$\text{P}(X = 19) = {}^{20}\text{C}_{1} \times 0.35 \times 0.65^{19}$$

$$\text{P}(X = 20) = 0.65^{20}$$

Why ${}^{20}\text{C}_{2}$ for 18 hits? Choosing which 18 shots hit is the same as choosing which 2 shots miss. In the same way ${}^{20}\text{C}_{1} = 20$ for 19 hits. (The printed mark scheme writes $19$ in the second term; that is a misprint, since ${}^{20}\text{C}_{1} = 20$ is what gives its stated total.)

**Work out each term**

First term: ${}^{20}\text{C}_{2} = \dfrac{20 \times 19}{2} = 190$, and $0.35^2 = 0.1225$.

$$190 \times 0.1225 \times 0.65^{18} = 23.275 \times 0.000428983 = 0.009985$$

Second term: $20 \times 0.35 = 7$.

$$7 \times 0.65^{19} = 7 \times 0.000278839 = 0.001952$$

Third term:

$$0.65^{20} = 0.000181$$

Calculator shortcut: use the binomial pdf (or the cumulative function: $1 - \text{P}(X \leqslant 17)$) with $n = 20$, $p = 0.65$.

**Add them up (A1)**

$$\text{P}(X \geqslant 18) = 0.009985 + 0.001952 + 0.000181 = 0.012118$$

To 3 significant figures this is $0.0121$.

**Compare with the significance level (second M1)**

The significance level is 1%, which is $0.01$. The rule is: if the probability of a result this extreme is **smaller** than the significance level, reject $\text{H}_0$.

$$0.0121 > 0.01$$

Our probability is bigger than $0.01$, so the result is not unusual enough. We do **not** reject $\text{H}_0$.

**Conclusion in context (A1 ft)**

We never say we have 'proved' anything. We say what the evidence shows: at the 1% level there is not enough evidence that Jill's hit rate has improved from 65%. Her 18 out of 20 could reasonably be luck. Notice this is a close call, because 0.0121 is only just above 0.01.

**Final answer**

$\text{P}(X \geqslant 18) = 0.0121$ (3 s.f.), which is greater than $0.01$.

There is no evidence, at the 1% significance level, that Jill has improved (she has probably not improved).
